summary: Describes the techniques and mechanisms currently used to allocate and assign IP multicast addresses. Documentation had fallen out of date and this caused confusion, so this informational memo gives an overview of the multicast addressing architecture as it stood at the time.

plainLanguage.summary: Multicast is how one sender reaches many receivers at once, and it needs a group address that the receivers agree to join. This RFC sorts out how those addresses are actually obtained. It explains the difference between an operator obtaining a block of addresses and an application obtaining one group address, then lists every method in use for each job and says which ones work for IPv4, which for IPv6, and which were tried and abandoned.

questions: difference between multicast allocation and assignment
what is the difference between multicast allocation and assignment
subtitle: A survey of how multicast group addresses are handed out, and why the earlier picture was confusing.

tldr.problem: Good, up-to-date documentation of IP multicast was close to non-existent, and some of what existed was confusing or misleading, so people could not get a clear view of how multicast addressing actually worked.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC separates two jobs that were used interchangeably, allocation of blocks of addresses to operators and assignment of individual group addresses to applications, and then surveys every method used for each, with a table showing which apply to IPv4 and which to IPv6.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational snapshot that obsoletes RFC 2908 and re-classifies RFC 2908, RFC 2776 and RFC 2909 as Historic. It records that dynamic allocation protocols were abandoned as too complex and unnecessary.

today: RFC 6308 was published in June 2011 as an Informational document. It obsoletes RFC 2908 and re-classifies RFC 2908, RFC 2776 and RFC 2909 as Historic. It has not been obsoleted or updated since, so it remains a snapshot of the practice as it stood in 2011.

sections.title: Why This Overview Exists
sections.content:
Good, up-to-date documentation of IP multicast was close to non-existent. This was especially a problem for multicast address allocation, to networks and sites, and assignment, to hosts and applications. The problem was made worse by the existence of confusing or misleading documentation on the subject, and the consequence was that people who wanted to learn about IP multicast and how its addressing works did not get a clear view of the current situation.

The aim of this document is to give a brief overview of multicast addressing and of the allocation techniques. The term addressing architecture refers, in an informal way, to the set of addressing mechanisms and methods in use.

The RFC also notes the limits of its own scope. Source-Specific Multicast does not have these addressing problems, because SSM group addresses have only local significance, so the document concentrates on the Any Source Multicast model. Everything about allocation in this RFC is therefore about ASM; SSM needs no block allocation at all, though the question of assigning SSM addresses inside a node is still discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: The documentation on multicast addressing had fallen out of date and in places said the wrong thing, so people could not tell how it really worked. This memo is a snapshot of the practice at the time, written to correct the record.

sections.title: Allocation and Assignment Are Different Jobs
sections.content:
Almost all multicast documents, and many other RFCs such as DHCPv4 and DHCPv6, use the terms address allocation and address assignment interchangeably. The operator and address management communities use them for two conceptually different processes.

In unicast operations, address allocation refers to leasing a large block of addresses from IANA to a Regional Internet Registry, or from a Regional Internet Registry to a Local Internet Registry, possibly through a National Internet Registry. Address assignment, on the other hand, is the lease of smaller address blocks or even single addresses to the end-user sites or end users themselves.

The RFC therefore separates the two functions throughout: allocation describes how larger blocks of addresses are obtained by network operators, and assignment describes how applications, nodes, or sets of nodes obtain a multicast address for their own use.
sections.plainLanguage: Two different things were being called the same name. An operator gets a big block of addresses from the registry, and that is allocation. An application then gets one group address out of a block it is allowed to use, and that is assignment. Keeping the words apart makes the rest of the document easier to follow.

sections.title: How Operators Obtain Address Blocks
sections.content:
Four families of method are described for allocating blocks of multicast addresses to operators.

Derived allocation takes the unicast prefix, or some other property of the network such as its autonomous system number, and computes the multicast block from it. GLOP allocation inserts the 16-bit public AS number in the middle of the IPv4 multicast prefix 233.0.0.0/8, so each AS number gets a /24 worth of multicast addresses. That is enough for multicast testing or small-scale use, but perhaps not for extensive use. The RFC notes a debugging problem with GLOP: the connection between the AS and the prefix is not apparent from the prefix when the AS number is greater than 255, but has to be calculated, as AS 5662 maps to 233.22.30.0/24. GLOP is also not available with 4-byte AS numbers, and no GLOP algorithm has been defined for IPv6.

For IPv6, unicast-prefix-based allocation embeds up to 64 high-order bits of an IPv6 unicast address in the prefix part of the multicast address, leaving at least 32 bits of group-id space after the mapping. The IPv6 Embedded Rendezvous Point technique builds on this by embedding the unicast prefix and interface identifier of the PIM-SM rendezvous point in the prefix, so that routing systems have everything they need to run the group. The RFC calls the IPv6 unicast-prefix-based allocations an extremely useful way for each network operator, even each subnet, to obtain multicast addresses easily, through an easy computation. A similar IPv4 mapping exists but gives only a limited number of addresses, for example one per IPv4 /24 block.

Administratively scoped allocation is provided in IPv4 under 239.0.0.0/8, and in IPv6 by 4-bit encoding in the multicast address prefix. The IPv4 prefix divides into Local Scope at 239.255.0.0/16 and Organization Local Scope at 239.192.0.0/14. Groups shared between multiple routing domains are more problematic and typically need a global multicast address, because their scope is undefined. Static IANA allocation is possible in rare cases, for blocks of up to 256 addresses directly from IANA. Dynamic allocation protocols, such as the Multicast Address-Set Claim Protocol and the Multicast Address Allocation Protocol, were complex, were never deployed or seriously implemented, and the RFC concludes that they provide no benefit beyond the GLOP and unicast-prefix-based mechanisms and have been abandoned.
sections.plainLanguage: An operator can work out its own block of group addresses from something it already owns, such as its network address or its routing domain number. That is the common approach. Some operators also hold a block from the central registry for their internal use, and a few held one straight from IANA. Protocols that let a machine ask for addresses at runtime were designed twice, were complicated, and were never used.

sections.title: How a Group Address Is Assigned
sections.content:
Assignment is how an application, node, or set of nodes learns the multicast address it should use.

Derived assignment has far fewer options than derived allocation. It has only been specified for IPv6 link-scoped multicast, where the EUI64 is embedded in the multicast address, giving a node unique multicast addresses for link-local ASM communications. For SSM, group addresses have only local significance to the node, but there is still a question of how to assign addresses between the applications running on the same IP address. The RFC does not consider this a problem, because the addresses are typically chosen manually or statically, though an API could check for conflicts before handing one out.

Manually configured assignment is the most common technique when the application has no static IANA assignment. A user asks the network operator for an address by phone or email, and the operator provides one, which the user then configures into the application by hand. The method works when the number of participants in a group is small, since each one has to be configured by hand.

Static IANA assignment means getting an assignment for a particular application directly from IANA, in one of two forms. Global assignment is seen as lucrative because it is the simplest approach for application developers, who can hard-code the multicast address, needing no lease and no service discovery, but it has an architectural scaling problem, because it encourages a land-grab of the limited multicast address space. Scope-relative assignment instead gives a number as an integer offset from the highest address in each IPv4 administrative scope: the SLPv2 discovery scope-relative offset is 2, so its discovery address within IPv4 Local-Scope is 239.255.255.253, and within IPv4 Organization Local-Scope it is 239.195.255.253.

Dynamic assignment mechanisms also exist. MADCAP describes assignment from Multicast Address Allocation Servers to applications and nodes, and DHCPv6 assignment has been proposed, but neither has gained traction, and it is not clear whether the sparse deployment is due to a lack of need. The Session Announcement Protocol takes a different approach, advertising global multicast sessions and associating ranges of addresses with them so that SAP-aware applications can create new groups, but creating a session is a tedious process and the IPv6 SAP address is unroutable in inter-domain multicast. The RFC draws four conclusions: multicast is not significantly attractive in the first place; most applications have a static IANA assignment and so need no dynamic or manual assignment; the applications that could not be easily satisfied with an IANA or manual assignment are marginal; and there are other reasons dynamic assignments are not seen as useful, such as issues related to service discovery and rendezvous.
sections.plainLanguage: An application that wants to receive a group usually asks its network operator for an address and types it in by hand. Applications with a large audience instead get a fixed address from the central registry and hard-code it, which is simple but eats into a small pool of addresses. Schemes that hand out addresses automatically were built but never widely used.

sections.title: What the Survey Concludes
sections.content:
The RFC summarises its findings for prefix allocation. Only ASM is affected by the allocation and assignment issues. With IPv4, GLOP provides a sufficient allocation mechanism for holders of a 16-bit AS number, IPv4 unicast-prefix-based allocation offers some addresses, IANA is also allocating from the AD-HOC block III, formerly called EGLOP, especially with 32-bit AS number holders in mind, and administratively scoped allocations provide the opportunity for internal IPv4 allocations. With IPv6, unicast-prefix-based addresses and their derivatives provide a good allocation strategy, and this also works for scoped multicast addresses. Dynamic allocations, the RFC concludes, are too complex and unnecessary a mechanism.

For address assignment, manually configured assignment is typical today and works to a sufficient degree at smaller scale. Global IANA assignment has been done extensively in the past. Scope-relative IANA assignment is acceptable, but the size of the pool is not very high, and inter-domain routing of IPv6 IANA-assigned prefixes is likely to be challenging, so the approach is not very appealing. Dynamic assignment has been implemented but has no wide deployment, which suggests either that there are other gaps in the multicast architecture or that there was never enough demand for it. Derived assignments are only applicable in a fringe case of link-scoped multicast.

The RFC lists three future actions. Multicast address discovery and rendezvous need to be analysed at more length and an adequate solution provided. The IETF should consider whether to specify more ranges of the IPv4 administratively scoped address space for static allocation, for applications that should not be routed over the Internet, such as backup software, so that they would not need to use global addresses, which should never leak in any case. And the IETF should consider tightening its static IANA allocations policy, for example to the stricter policy of IETF Consensus, while looking at developing the discovery and rendezvous functions if necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: The short version is that computing an address from something you already own works well, asking for one by hand works well at small scale, and everything cleverer has not been used. The RFC asks for work on finding and joining groups, and for more of the private IPv4 address space to be set aside for local use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is explicit that it only describes approaches to allocating and assigning multicast addresses and that this has no security considerations of its own. The security analysis of the protocols it mentions is out of scope.

It adds one point: the dynamic assignment protocols in particular are inherently vulnerable to resource exhaustion attacks, as discussed in the specification of the Multicast Address Dynamic Client Allocation Protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC leaves security to the protocols it describes. Its one warning is that a protocol which hands out addresses on request can be attacked by asking for too many.

items.text: Multicast address discovery needs to be analysed at more length and an adequate solution provided.

items.text: Consider specifying more ranges of the IPv4 administratively scoped address space for static allocation to applications that should not be routed over the Internet.

items.text: Consider locking down the static IANA allocations policy, and look at developing the discovery and rendezvous functions if needed.
